To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified a cDNA clone encoding CSase from C. vulgaris by genetic complementation, and that the CSase of C. vulgarus is a member of the plant CSase superfamily, which is divided into three families, the plant CSases A family, the CSases B family and the CSases C family.
the CSase gene was cloned and characterized from a watermelon (C. vulgaris) cDNA library by genetic complementation of E. coli Cys− mutant cells.

we isolated a cDNA encoding a plant cytoplasmic cysteine synthases from an expression library of watermelon by genetic complementation of E. coli cysteine auxotropic mutant and that the deduced amino acid sequence is highly conserved in plants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation and characterization of a cDNA clone for CSase from C. vulgaris.
the isolation and molecular characterization of the cDNA encoding CSase from C. vulgaris.
the molecular cloning and expression of the cDNA for a cytoplasmic CSase from C. vulgaris.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the plant CSase superfamily consists of three families: plant CSase A, plant CSase B and bacterial CSase.
the CSases from plants belong to the CSase super family and are divided into the CSase A and B families.
the CSase A family is a unique group of proteins that are conserved in plant species and that the CSase B family is the group of CSases that are most closely related to the bacterial CSase proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have cloned a cDNA for a plant cysteine synthetase A, which is a member of the CSase super-family, and that we have shown that the CSase A is the most conserved member in the CSase gene family.
we have successfully cloned and characterized the gene encoding CSase A in watermelon, and the CSase A family of plant CSase proteins is evolutionarily the most conserved.
we have isolated a cDNA clone encoding the plant CSase superfamily, and have demonstrated that the cysA gene is expressed in the etiolated and green seedlings of C.vulgaris.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the plant CSase superfamily consists of three families and that the plant CSases in the CSase A family have a common ancestor.
CSase A is a member of the superfamily of O-acetylserine(thiol)lyases, which includes the enzymes cystathionine γ-synthase, cystathionine β-synthase, and cysteine synthases A, B and C.
CSases are not only involved in cysteine synthesis in plants but are also involved in the synthesis of β-pyrazolalanine, which is a precursor to the pyrazole alkaloids, in bacteria.
